questions.question: Explain what rust is, the conditions needed for iron to rust, and why corrosion matters.
questions.expected_answer: Rust is iron oxide, a flaky red-brown compound formed when iron reacts with oxygen in the presence of water; both oxygen and water are needed, so iron stays sound in dry air or under oil but rusts quickly in damp air and faster still where salt is present, as at the coast. Rust occupies more volume than the iron, so it lifts and flakes, exposing fresh metal and continuing until the metal is eaten through. Corrosion matters because it seizes hinges, makes roofs leak, weakens car bodies and swells reinforcing bars so that concrete cracks, costing billions of rand a year in repair and replacement. All preservation methods work by keeping oxygen and water away from the metal.

questions.question: Describe how painting preserves steel, including surface preparation, and state its advantages and its main weakness.
questions.expected_answer: Paint is a barrier: a film of pigment in a binder that dries to a tough skin, sealing the surface so oxygen and water cannot reach the iron. The steel is first cleaned of rust, scale and grease by brushing, sanding or blasting, then given a primer, often containing a rust-inhibiting pigment, that grips the metal, followed by top coats for weather and colour. Advantages: cheap, available in any colour, and applied on site by brush, roller or spray to objects of any size. Weakness: it is only a skin, so wherever it is chipped, scratched or worn the bare metal rusts and the rust spreads beneath the paint, lifting it; paint also chalks and cracks in sunlight and must be renewed every few years.

questions.question: Describe hot-dip galvanising and explain sacrificial protection, then compare galvanising with painting.
questions.expected_answer: In hot-dip galvanising, cleaned steel is dipped in molten zinc at about 450 degrees and emerges with a bonded grey zinc coat, used on wire, sheet, pipe, bolts, posts, roofing and pylons. The zinc acts as a barrier like paint, but because zinc is more reactive than iron, when the coat is scratched and wetted a small electric cell forms in which the zinc corrodes instead of the exposed steel, so the scratch does not rust; this is sacrificial protection. The zinc is slowly consumed, lasting thirty to fifty years inland and less at the coast where salt speeds its loss. Compared with paint, galvanising lasts far longer and protects at breaks, but is a single grey colour, must be done in a factory bath, cannot easily be repaired on site, and costs more initially; paint is cheap, colourful and applied anywhere, but fails at every break and needs renewal.
